advances: The universal actual-parity refined stock inequality fails for every choice of positive absolute small-core, small-atom, and stock-ratio thresholds, even on exact no-Boolean private-label supports whose double-point graph in every parity and probability band is a star. This is a counterexample to that auxiliary aggregation bridge. On the same examples the direct band sum, and both original cubics after multiplication by the canonical factor \(Q^3\), tend to infinity; no disproof of either original cubic bound or of the locked weak Oertel conjecture follows.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The distinct-coefficient label multiplicity estimate is consumed only as an accepted assertion of cad0388c41d8cdc7. Every other assertion, including the cutoff layer, the new group-size normalization, the support census, all actual parity and midpoint counts, the all-scales star property, and the direct cubic calibration, is proved above.
proof:
The only mathematical input from accepted fact cad0388c41d8cdc7 is its bound \(M_{\max}\le C_0 2^m/\sqrt m\), proved there from distinct-coefficient Sárközy-Szemerédi concentration. Its active coefficients specialize to \(h_a=a\), and its full label family is exactly the family used before the cutoff here. Deleting labels can only reduce each multiplicity. In particular, this use concerns the original label census and is independent of the private-group cardinalities. We prove all geometry, normalization, and band assertions for the new cardinalities directly.

First prove (1). There are \(M_{\rm tot}=m2^{m-1}\) labels. Conditional on the distinguished index \(i\), take the remaining \(b_a\) to be independent fair bits and set
$$
X_i:=\sum_{a\ne i}a(b_a-1/2),\qquad
\mu_i:=T_m/2+3i/2,\qquad e_q=\mu_i+X_i,\qquad
\sigma_i^2:=\mathbb E X_i^2=\frac14\sum_{a\ne i}a^2.
\tag{10}
$$
The law of \(X_i\) is symmetric. For \(m\ge6\),
$$
\frac{m^3}{24}\le\sigma_i^2\le\frac{m^3}{4},\qquad
\mathbb E X_i^4
=3\sigma_i^4-2\sum_{a\ne i}(a/2)^4\le3\sigma_i^4.
\tag{11}
$$
Indeed \(\sum_{a=1}^m a^2\ge m^3/3\), deletion removes at most \(m^2\), and \(\sum_{a=1}^m a^2\le m^3\). Cauchy's inequality applied on the event \(|X_i|\ge\sigma_i/\sqrt2\) gives
$$
\sigma_i^2\le\frac{\sigma_i^2}{2}
+\left(\mathbb E X_i^4\,\mathbb P\lbrace |X_i|\ge\sigma_i/\sqrt2\rbrace\right)^{1/2}.
$$
Thus the probability in this display is at least \(1/12\). Symmetry gives \(\mathbb P(X_i\le-\sigma_i/\sqrt2)\ge1/24\). For \(m\ge256\), (11) implies \(\sigma_i/\sqrt2\ge m^{3/2}/\sqrt{48}>3m/2\), so this latter event forces \(e_q<T_m/2\). Put \(W=4m^{3/2}\). Since \(\mu_i\ge T_m/2\), Chebyshev's inequality also gives
$$
\mathbb P(e_q<T_m/2-W)\le\mathbb P(X_i<-W)
\le\frac{\sigma_i^2}{W^2}\le\frac1{64}.
$$
Consequently, for each \(i\), at least a fraction \(1/24-1/64=5/192\) of its labels have energy in \([T_m/2-W,T_m/2)\). For \(m=2^{4d}\), both \(T_m/2\) and \(W\) are integers. This interval contains exactly \(W\) integer energies. Summing over \(i\) and pigeonholing gives an integer \(H\) in the interval with
$$
M_H\ge\frac{(5/192)m2^{m-1}}{4m^{3/2}}
=\frac5{1536}\frac{2^m}{\sqrt m}
\ge c_*\frac{2^m}{\sqrt m}.
\tag{12}
$$
In particular \(H<T_m/2\). For any \(H\le T_m/2\), symmetry in (10) gives \(\mathbb P(e_q\ge\mu_i)\ge1/2\) and \(\mu_i\ge H\), hence at least half of all labels have \(e_q\ge H\). This proves the tail assertion in (1).

For all sufficiently large \(m\), the multiplicity bound makes \(2^{m+1}/M_H\ge2\sqrt m/C_0\ge1\). Rounding this number upward to a power of two multiplies it by a factor strictly less than two. Together with (12), this proves (2). All group cardinalities in (3) are therefore finite positive even integers, at least two. There are finitely many labels and finite maximal energy \(T_m+m\), so \(L\) and all dimensions in (4) are finite integers as well.

We next determine the complete support without making any assumption about its Boolean part. For each retained \(q\), let \(F_q\) consist of the points with active vector \(d_q\), binary neutral coordinates, and at least two neutral ones in \(G_q\). Let \(B_{\rm act}=D\cap\lbrace0,1\rbrace^k\). The exact disjoint decomposition is
$$
D=B_{\rm act}\mathbin{\dot\cup}\coprod_{q\in\mathcal Q_0}(E_q\mathbin{\dot\cup}F_q),\qquad
D_2=E,\qquad D_1=B_{\rm act}\mathbin{\dot\cup}\coprod_{q\in\mathcal Q_0}F_q.
\tag{13}
$$
To prove it, all generator coordinates lie between zero and two. If an integral convex combination has an active two in coordinate \(i\), every positive-coefficient generator has that same active two. The other active coordinates of those generators are binary; integrality of their averages forces agreement in each coordinate. Thus all generators in the combination have one label \(q\). No point can have two active twos. If all neutral coordinates of the point are binary, their sum in \(G_q\) is at least two, because every generator has that property. Conversely, any binary neutral vector with two specified ones in \(G_q\) is the midpoint of two \(E_q\) points: replace those ones \((1,1)\) by \((2,0)\) and \((0,2)\), leaving all other coordinates fixed. This proves precisely the \(F_q\) assertion.

If an integral point has a neutral two at coordinate \(v\in G_q\), every positive-coefficient generator must have a two there. The private-group disjointness forces them all to belong to \(E_q\) and to have their neutral two at \(v\). All other neutral coordinates are binary, so their integral averages are binary and the resulting point belongs to \(E_q\). This also excludes two neutral twos and a neutral two with no active two. Every remaining integral point is Boolean. Distinct labels have distinct active vectors, proving disjointness in (13). This proves the ternary and at-most-two-twos assertions. Finally \(E\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(E)\) gives \(\operatorname{conv}(D)=\operatorname{conv}(E)\), and hence \(D=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^k\), which is completeness. The appended zero coordinate in \(A\) changes none of these conclusions.

Every generator has affine active energy at least \(H\). Therefore every point of \(\operatorname{conv}(E)\), and in particular every point of \(D\) including \(B_{\rm act}\), has active energy at least \(H\). This observation supplies a weight bound for the actual Boolean core without identifying it explicitly.

For the normalization, write
$$
K_0:=2^{L-H},\qquad P:=\frac{Z}{\nu K_0},\qquad
a_r:=\max(2^{-r},\delta),\qquad
U_1:=\sum_{r\ge0}M_{H+r}a_r,\qquad
U_2:=\sum_{r\ge0}M_{H+r}a_r^2.
\tag{14}
$$
All sums are finite. The scalar \(K_0\) is the same expression \(2^{L-H}\) called \(K\) in cad0388c41d8cdc7; its role here does not assert equal label masses. For a label of energy \(H+r\), its \(g_r\) choices of the neutral-two position have disjoint endpoint sets of size \(2^{L-1}\), and all endpoint weights equal \(2^{-H-r}\). Thus
$$
|E_q|=g_r2^{L-1},\qquad
\sum_{x\in E_q}w_x=g_r2^{L-1-H-r}=\nu K_0 a_r,\qquad
\sum_{x\in E}w_x=\nu K_0U_1.
\tag{15}
$$
Here the identity \(a_r=2^{\max(0,r-J)-r}\) handles \(r=J\) exactly.

Put \(f(n)=1-(n+1)2^{-n}\). Counting binary private coordinates gives \(|F_q|=2^L f(n_q)\). In particular \(f(n)\le1\), and the total weight of all \(F_q\) is at most \(K_0\sum_{r\ge0}M_{H+r}2^{-r}\le2K_0M_{\max}\). Also \(|B_{\rm act}|\le2^{m+L}\), and every one of its points has weight at most \(2^{-H}\). Hence its total weight is at most \(K_02^m\). Equation (13) now yields the exact endpoint mass and the bounds
$$
p(E)=\frac{U_1}{P}=1-\alpha,\qquad
U_1\le P\le U_1+\frac{2M_{\max}+2^m}{\nu},\qquad
\alpha\le\frac{2M_{\max}+2^m}{\nu U_1}.
\tag{16}
$$
No probabilities in these estimates are conditional probabilities.

The inequalities \(a_r\ge\delta\), \(a_r\le\delta+2^{-r}\), and \(a_r^2\le\delta^2+4^{-r}\) give
$$
\begin{aligned}
U_1&\ge\delta R\ge\tfrac14m^{1/4}2^m,\\
U_1&\le\delta M_{\rm tot}+2M_{\max}
\le(\tfrac12+2C_0)m^{1/4}2^m,\\
U_2&\le\delta^2M_{\rm tot}+\tfrac43M_{\max}
\le A_2\,\frac{2^m}{\sqrt m},\qquad A_2:=\tfrac12+\tfrac43C_0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{17}
$$
For a convenient absolute constant \(A_3:=1+4C_0+2C_0^2\), equations (2), (16), and (17) imply
$$
\tfrac14m^{1/4}2^m\le P\le A_3m^{1/4}2^m,\qquad
\alpha\le2C_0(1+2C_0)m^{-3/4}.
\tag{18}
$$
For example, the extra term in the upper bound for \(P\) is at most \((C_0/2+C_0^2)2^m\) for \(m\ge1\), which is covered by \(A_3\). Since every point of \(D\) has energy at least \(H\), (5) also gives
$$
Q\max_{x\in D}p_x\le\frac{2^{m+L-H}}{Z}
=\frac{2^m}{\nu P}\le2C_0m^{-3/4}.
\tag{19}
$$
The elementary inequality \(\sum_xp_x^4\le(\max_xp_x)^3\sum_xp_x\) consequently proves \(S_4Q^3\le8C_0^3m^{-9/4}\). For all sufficiently large \(d\), (19) is at most \(2^{-10}\), so every endpoint lies in a retained band of (6). This proves both smallness assertions in (7) and full endpoint retention.

We compute actual parities and distinct midpoint images for those bands. Each occupied integer endpoint energy \(e=H+r\) has probability \(p_e=2^{-e}/Z\). The half-open interval \((t_j/2,t_j]\) can contain at most one such energy: probabilities for different integer energies differ by a power of two, and the two endpoints of a ratio-two interval cannot both be included. Every occupied energy has a band after full retention. If \(j\) is that band, then \(\gamma=t_j/p_e\) belongs to \([1,2)\). Its value is common to all occupied endpoint energies, since the ratios for any two energies and indices differ by an integral power of two and both lie in \([1,2)\). This argument includes exact dyadic boundary equalities.

At a fixed energy, two labels with equal active parity have the same \(b\); equality of their energies then gives \(2i=2i'\), so the labels coincide. Within a label \(q\), the occupied neutral parities are exactly the binary vectors having at least one zero in \(G_q\): the neutral two has to occupy such a zero, and each such parity can be realized. Distinct labels at the same energy have disjoint active parity classes. Therefore, with \(g_r\) as in (3), the exact count is
$$
q_j=2^LM_{H+r}(1-2^{-g_r})\ge\tfrac34\,2^LM_{H+r}.
\tag{20}
$$
This uses \(g_r\ge2\) and counts only actual endpoint parities.

Distinct same-parity endpoints in a band must lie in the same label. If their neutral twos were at the same position, equality of parity would fix every other binary coordinate and the endpoints would coincide. Their two positions are therefore different; at each such position the other endpoint has zero. All other neutral coordinates agree. Their midpoint is precisely a point of \(F_q\). Conversely, the two-endpoint construction proving (13) has distinct same-parity endpoints, so every \(F_q\) point occurs. Thus the complete deduplicated midpoint image and all masses are
$$
\begin{aligned}
C_j&=\coprod_{q:e_q=H+r}F_q,
&|C_j|&=2^LM_{H+r}f(g_r),\\
m_j&=\frac{M_{H+r}a_r}{P},
&\omega_j&=\frac{\gamma M_{H+r}2^{-r}f(g_r)}{\nu P}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
$$
In particular every occupied band has positive midpoint stock, because \(f(2)=1/4\) and \(f(n+1)-f(n)=n2^{-n-1}>0\) for \(n\ge1\).

At energy \(H\) the endpoint count is \(\nu M_H2^L\). The choice of \(\nu\) makes this at least \(2^{m+1}2^L=2Q\). Its retained band, denoted \(j(H)\), therefore belongs to \(\mathcal J\). Using (12), (2), (18), (21), \(\gamma\ge1\), and \(f(2\nu)\ge1/4\) gives
$$
\Omega\ge\omega_{j(H)}\ge\frac{M_H}{4\nu P}
\ge\frac{c_*^2}{16A_3}\,m^{-5/4}>0.
\tag{22}
$$
On the other hand (20)-(21), summed over the actual dense subset, yield
$$
\Gamma\le\frac{4}{3}\frac{2^m}{P^2}
\sum_{r\ge0}M_{H+r}a_r^2
\le\frac{64A_2}{3m}.
\tag{23}
$$
Together (22)-(23) prove the ratio estimate (7). In particular, choosing \(d\) large enough makes all three residual quantities simultaneously smaller than any prescribed positive thresholds, proving the stated counterexample quantifiers.

The graph property follows directly from the same geometry. Any point contributing an edge has exactly two coordinates equal to two, hence belongs to \(E\) by (13). Its edge consists of one active coordinate \(i\) and one neutral coordinate in \(G_{(b,i)}\), where \(b\) is the active part of \(\xi\). For this fixed active parity \(b\), the energy associated with \(i\) is \(\sum_a a b_a+2i\). Two different active coordinates give energies differing by at least two and probabilities differing by a factor at least four. They cannot lie together in any one half-open ratio-two probability interval, for any choice of \(\lambda\) and \(\ell\). Hence a nonempty graph fixes the active coordinate \(i\), and every edge contains it. No theorem about this graph class is being assumed.

It remains to verify the direct calibration (9). The largest label energy is \(e_{\max}=T_m+m\), and exactly one label attains it: \(i=m\), \(b_m=0\), and \(b_a=1\) for every \(a\ne m\). Indeed for index \(i\) the largest possible energy is \(T_m+i\), with equality only when all other bits are one. Put \(r_{\max}=e_{\max}-H\). Since \(H\le T_m/2\), we have \(r_{\max}\ge T_m/2+m\). Thus \(r_{\max}\ge J\) for all sufficiently large \(d\). Its endpoint band has cardinality \(\nu2^{r_{\max}-J}2^L\); its ratio to \(2Q\) is at least \(\nu2^{T_m/2-J-1}\), which tends to infinity. This band is therefore dense and is retained by (19).

For that band write \(g=g_{r_{\max}}\), \(u=1-2^{-g}\), and \(\gamma=t_j/p_{e_{\max}}\). Equations (20)-(21) have \(M_{e_{\max}}=1\) and \(a_{r_{\max}}=\delta\), so its exact contribution to \(Q^3\Psi\) is
$$
Q^3\frac{m_j^6}{q_j^3\omega_j^2}
=\frac{8^m\nu^2\delta^6\,4^{r_{\max}}}
{\gamma^2P^4u^3f(g)^2}
\ge\frac{8^m\nu^2\delta^6\,4^{r_{\max}}}{4P^4}.
\tag{24}
$$
Here \(1\le\gamma<2\) and \(0<u,f(g)\le1\). By (2), (18), \(\delta^6=m^{-9/2}\), and \(2r_{\max}\ge T_m+2m\), the last expression is at least
$$
\frac{1}{C_0^2A_3^4}\,m^{-9/2}2^{T_m+m},
\tag{25}
$$
which tends to infinity. This already proves the first conclusion of (9).

For completeness, the link from the direct band sum to both original cubics is proved here for these exact supports and the original law. If \(x,y\in D\) have integral midpoint \(c\), completeness puts \(c\in D\) and affinity of (5) gives \(p_c^2=p_xp_y\). For a band \(j\in\mathcal J\), let \(n_{b,j}\) be its endpoint count of parity \(b\) and set \(v_j=\sum_b n_{b,j}(n_{b,j}-1)\), the number of ordered distinct same-parity pairs. Cauchy's inequality and \(n_j\ge2Q\ge2q_j\) give
$$
v_j\ge n_j^2/q_j-n_j\ge n_j^2/(2q_j)>0.
\tag{26}
$$
For \(c\in C_j\), let \(R_j(c)\) be the sum of \(\min(p_x,p_y)\) over these ordered distinct pairs with midpoint \(c\). Distinct unordered pairs reflected about \(c\) have disjoint endpoint sets. Every closed affine halfspace containing \((c,0)\) contains at least one endpoint of each such pair, including when the center lies on its boundary. Thus \(\tau_p((c,0))\ge R_j(c)/2\). Also the full ordered reflection sum \(s_p(c)\) is at least \(R_j(c)\). These assertions are unchanged if the allowed halfspaces are required to have a nonzero normal.

Put \(r_j=|C_j|\). By affinity and the band bounds,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{c\in C_j}p_c^{1/3}R_j(c)
&=\sum_{\substack{x,y\in E_j,\ x\ne y\\x\equiv y\pmod2}}
\min(p_x,p_y)^{7/6}\max(p_x,p_y)^{1/6}\\
&\ge(t_j/2)^{4/3}v_j.
\end{aligned}
$$
Hölder's inequality bounds the cube of the left side by \(r_j^2\sum_{c\in C_j}p_cR_j(c)^3\). Using (26), \(m_j\le t_jn_j\), and \(\omega_j=t_jr_j\), we obtain
$$
\sum_{c\in C_j}p_cR_j(c)^3
\ge\frac{t_j^4v_j^3}{16r_j^2}
\ge\frac{t_j^4n_j^6}{128q_j^3r_j^2}
\ge\frac{m_j^6}{128q_j^3\omega_j^2}.
\tag{27}
$$
Every midpoint in \(C_j\) has probability in \((t_j/2,t_j]\), by \(p_c^2=p_xp_y\), so these midpoint images for different \(j\) are disjoint, including at band boundaries. Summing (27) and the preceding halfspace and reflection bounds proves
$$
M_3(p)\ge\Psi/1024,\qquad T(p)\ge\Psi/128.
\tag{28}
$$
Equations (25) and (28) give the remaining conclusions in (9). Thus the failed quantity is the universal \(\Gamma/\Omega\) aggregation bound, while the direct band sum and the original cubic lower bounds survive with arbitrarily large normalized values on this particular family.
statement:
There is a sequence of finite complete ternary sets \(D\) in dimension \(k\), with at most two coordinates equal to two at every point, and original affine-exponential probability laws \(p\), having the following properties. All limits below are along positive integers \(d\) tending to infinity.

Set \(m=2^{4d}\), \(J=3d\), and \(\delta=2^{-J}=m^{-3/4}\). The energy total is \(T_m=m(m+1)/2\). For active coordinates \(a=1,\ldots,m\), set \(h_a=a\). Before the cutoff, labels are all pairs \(q=(b,i)\) with \(b\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^m\), \(i\in\lbrace1,\ldots,m\rbrace\), and \(b_i=0\). Their active vectors and integer energies are
$$
d_q=b+2\mathbf e_i,\qquad e_q=\sum_{a=1}^m a b_a+2i,\qquad
M_e=|\lbrace q:e_q=e\rbrace|,\qquad M_{\max}=\max_e M_e.
$$
Let \(C_0\ge4\) be the absolute constant in the label multiplicity bound of accepted fact cad0388c41d8cdc7, so that \(M_{\max}\le C_0 2^m/\sqrt m\). For every sufficiently large \(d\), choose an integer \(H\) satisfying
$$
H\le\lfloor T_m/2\rfloor,\qquad
M_H\ge c_*\frac{2^m}{\sqrt m},\qquad
R:=\sum_{e\ge H}M_e\ge m2^{m-2},\qquad c_*:=2^{-9}.
\tag{1}
$$
Such an \(H\) exists by the elementary argument in the proof. Retain exactly the labels in \(\mathcal Q_0=\lbrace q:e_q\ge H\rbrace\). Let \(\nu\) be the smallest number of the form \(2^s\), \(s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), that is at least \(2^{m+1}/M_H\). For all sufficiently large \(d\), this gives
$$
\frac{2}{C_0}\sqrt m\le\nu<\frac{4}{c_*}\sqrt m.
\tag{2}
$$
For each retained label \(q\), take a private group \(G_q\) of \(n_q\) neutral coordinates, with all groups disjoint, where
$$
n_q=g_{e_q-H},\qquad g_r:=2\nu\,2^{\max(0,r-J)}\quad(r\ge0),\qquad
L:=\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q_0}n_q,\qquad k:=m+L,\qquad N:=k+1,\qquad Q:=2^k.
\tag{3}
$$
Let \(E_q\) be the set of points in \(\mathbb Z^k\) with active vector \(d_q\), exactly one neutral coordinate equal to two, that coordinate in \(G_q\), and every other neutral coordinate independently in \(\lbrace0,1\rbrace\). Define exactly
$$
E:=\bigcup_{q\in\mathcal Q_0}E_q,\qquad
D:=\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^k,\qquad A:=D\times\lbrace0\rbrace\subseteq\mathbb R^N.
\tag{4}
$$
No Boolean points are adjoined. The field, weights, normalizer, and probabilities are
$$
\beta=((a\log2)_{a=1}^m,0,\ldots,0),\qquad
w_x=\exp(-\beta\cdot x),\qquad Z=\sum_{x\in D}w_x,\qquad
p_x=p_{(x,0)}=w_x/Z.
\tag{5}
$$
The support, field, original law, and band notation here have exactly their meanings in cad0388c41d8cdc7. The new group sizes (3) replace that fact's exponentially compensated group sizes, and no equal-label-mass assertion or conclusion of its refined stock theorem is invoked.

Use the canonical actual core and bands
$$
\begin{aligned}
D_1&=\lbrace x\in D:\#\lbrace a:x_a=2\rbrace\le1\rbrace,
&D_2&=D\setminus D_1,
&\alpha&=p(D_1),
&S_4&=\sum_{x\in D}p_x^4,\\
t_0&=2^{-10}/Q,
&t_j&=t_02^{-j}\quad(j\ge0),
&E_j&=\lbrace x\in D_2:t_j/2<p_x\le t_j\rbrace,\\
n_j&=|E_j|,
&m_j&=p(E_j),
&\mathcal J&=\lbrace j\ge0:n_j\ge2Q\rbrace,\\
q_j&=|\lbrace x\bmod2:x\in E_j\rbrace|,
&C_j&=\lbrace (x+y)/2:x,y\in E_j,\ x\ne y,\ x\equiv y\pmod2\rbrace,\\
\omega_j&=t_j|C_j|,
&\Gamma&=\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}\frac{m_j^2Q}{q_j},
&\Omega&=\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}\omega_j.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
$$
For all sufficiently large \(d\), the entire set \(D_2\) is retained in these bands, the band of energy \(H\) belongs to \(\mathcal J\), and \(\Omega>0\). The quantitative conclusions are
$$
\alpha=O(m^{-3/4}),\qquad S_4Q^3=O(m^{-9/4}),\qquad
\Gamma=O(m^{-1}),\qquad \Omega\ge c\,m^{-5/4},\qquad
\frac{\Gamma^3}{\Omega^2}=O(m^{-1/2})\longrightarrow0,
\tag{7}
$$
with absolute implied constants and an absolute \(c>0\). Consequently, for every \(a_0,b_0,\eta>0\) there is a finite example (4)-(5) with \(\alpha<a_0\), \(S_4Q^3<b_0\), \(\Omega>0\), and \(\Gamma^3/\Omega^2<\eta\).

In fact these examples satisfy the following graph restriction at every scale. For a parity vector \(\xi\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^k\), put \(V_\xi=\lbrace u:\xi_u=0\rbrace\). For every \(\lambda>0\) and every integer \(\ell\), form the simple graph on \(V_\xi\) with an edge \(\lbrace u,v\rbrace\), \(u\ne v\), precisely when \(x=\xi+2\mathbf e_u+2\mathbf e_v\) belongs to \(D\) and \(\lambda2^{-\ell-1}<p_x\le\lambda2^{-\ell}\). Every nonempty such graph has a vertex common to all its edges. Here the standard basis vectors are in the full coordinate space \(\mathbb R^k\); in the label definition they are in the active block \(\mathbb R^m\).

There is also a direct calibration of what the counterexample does and does not obstruct. Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Psi&:=\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}\frac{m_j^6}{q_j^3\omega_j^2},\\
\tau_p(z)&:=\inf_{\substack{\mathcal H\text{ a closed affine halfspace in }\mathbb R^N\\z\in\mathcal H}}
\sum_{u\in A\cap\mathcal H}p_u,
&M_3(p)&:=\sum_{z\in A}p_z\tau_p(z)^3,\\
s_p(c)&:=\sum_{\substack{x,y\in D\\x+y=2c}}\min(p_x,p_y),
&T(p)&:=\sum_{c\in D}p_cs_p(c)^3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
$$
The reflection sum is over ordered pairs, with its diagonal counted once. The same conclusions hold if halfspaces in \(\tau_p\) must have a nonzero normal. Then
$$
Q^3\Psi\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
Q^3M_3(p)\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad Q^3T(p)\longrightarrow\infty.
\tag{9}
$$
